claims.claim: The deepest hole humans have ever dug (what a viewer has heard at second two: the Kola well is the deepest hole ever made)
claims.source_checked: Lobanov, Chicherov & Sharov 2021, doi:10.37482/issn2221-2698.2021.44.267: Russian PDF arcticandnorth.ru/upload/iblock/df4/267_284.pdf and the journal's English edition arcticandnorth.ru/upload/iblock/61f/44_224_239.pdf; Zhu & Huang 2026, nature.com/articles/s43247-026-03246-z
claims.note: Lobanov (EN p.231): 'In 1990, the maximum depth was reached — 12262 m, which has not been surpassed so far.' Zhu & Huang (Feb 2026): 'remains the deepest vertical borehole ever attempted' and 'The deepest penetration is the Russia's Kola Superdeep Borehole'; the newer wells they list are shallower (SDTK-1 10,910 m, X-1 11,156 m). 'Dug' for a drilled hole is a framing word. True as stated at second two.

claims.claim: ...was drilled with a bit narrower than a dinner plate.
claims.source_checked: Lobanov 2021 (EN and RU PDFs), text p.276/EN p.232 and Fig. 5v 'actual well construction' (rendered at 600 dpi); USGS OFR 86-517 (pubs.usgs.gov/of/1986/0517/report.pdf) drilling sections; Met API object 201074
claims.note: The 214 mm bit is real (Lobanov: 'a 46 m long multistage turbine at the bottom with a 214 mm drill bit'), and it is narrower than the Met's 25.6 cm dinner plate. But the sentence says the hole was drilled with that bit, and the viewer takes away that the hole is narrower than a plate. Lobanov Fig. 5v gives the actual construction: 'd 720 mm, 40 m' at the top, casing 'd 325 mm, 2000 m', casing 'd 245 mm, 8770 m', and open hole 'd 215,9 mm, 12262 m'. The top 2 km had to be bored wider than the 325 mm casing, and the top 40 m is 72 cm across, so the upper hole is wider than a dinner plate. USGS: 'The predominantly uncased hole (after 2 km)'. The USGS bit list also includes 'reamers (to increase the diameter of the hole)' of 295.3 mm. Fails A3/A4 as worded. Change the line to something like 'The deepest hole humans have ever dug was drilled, for most of its depth, with a bit narrower than a dinner plate.' Or name the bit without the hole: 'its drill bit was narrower than a dinner plate.' Add the casing programme (Lobanov Fig. 5v) to SOURCES item 2.

claims.claim: 21 CM BIT / narrower than a dinner plate (tag)
claims.source_checked: Lobanov 2021 EN p.232; USGS OFR 86-517 bit list (KC-212.7, ISM-214.3); Met API collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/201074
claims.note: The text names the bit, and that holds: 214 mm rounds to 21 cm, and USGS lists coring bits of 212.7 and 214.3 mm. The Met has 51.86.100 'Dinner plate', 'Diameter: 10 1/16 in. (25.6 cm)'. The loupe drawn next to this tag is a separate claim (n 4).

claims.claim: Loupe showing 'the hole seen from above' with a dinner plate dropped over it that covers it
claims.note: A6: the drawing shows the mouth of the hole as smaller than a dinner plate. The well head is 720 mm across to 40 m, and the bore is wider than the 325 mm casing to 2,000 m (Fig. 5v), so a plate would not cover it. Draw the bit (or a cross-section 'near the bottom') against the plate, not the hole seen from above, or label it so.

claims.claim: THE HOLE (label on a 21 cm black disc, 'the mouth of the hole'), then DINNER PLATE dropped over it
claims.note: Same problem as n 4. A disc 21 cm across labelled 'THE HOLE' says the hole is that wide. It is that wide only in the open-hole section (215.9 mm nominal, below 8,770 m per Fig. 5v, and even there oval and caverned). At the top it is 720 mm. Relabel the disc 'THE BIT' (or 'NEAR THE BOTTOM'), or show the bit photo instead. This also makes SOURCES item 2's statement 'the line and the labels name the bit' true, which today it is not.

claims.claim: 21 CM BIT / DINNER PLATE (plate 25.6 cm, Met 51.86.100, bit drawn to scale against it)
claims.note: The Met API gives accessionNumber '51.86.100', title 'Dinner plate', 'Diameter: 10 1/16 in. (25.6 cm)'. The code draws BORE_CM 21 against PLATE_CM, which is to scale. The label text is right; the 'THE HOLE' disc under it is n 5.

claims.claim: It took the Soviet Union about twenty years.
claims.note: Lobanov: 'Drilling was started on May 24, 1970'; 'In 1990, the maximum depth was reached — 12262 m'. Zhu & Huang: 'reaching 12,262 m between 1970 and 1989'. 19-20 years, so 'about twenty' holds. Both dates fall before the USSR ended in Dec 1991. Note: Zhu & Huang cite Lobanov (their ref. 29) for this paragraph, so 1990 has the better footing.

claims.claim: Year counter 1970 -> 1989, then '1989–90'; 'drilling since 1970'; '1970' -> '1989–90' with 'ABOUT 20 YEARS'
claims.note: 1970 start (Lobanov). The end is shown as 1989–90, which carries the disagreement between Zhu & Huang (1989) and Lobanov (1990). Lobanov also has 'As of 05/01/1991, the well depth was 12262 m'.

claims.claim: It goes down twelve kilometres.
claims.note: 12,262 m in both sources; 'twelve kilometres' rounds down.

claims.claim: Depth counter to '12,262 M' / '12,262 METRES'; '12 KM DOWN'; 'THE HOLE: 12 KM'
claims.note: 12,262 m exactly as in both sources.

claims.claim: And it never made it through the crust.
claims.source_checked: USGS OFR 86-517 p. ii-iii (text lines 'Crustal thickness...'); Zhu & Huang 2026; Lobanov 2021
claims.note: USGS: 'Crustal thickness in the vicinity of the corehole was shown to be about 40 km.' Zhu & Huang: 'Despite not penetrating the Moho'. Lobanov: down to 12 km 'the borehole passed through gneisses and amphibolites of the Kola series, i.e. through the "granite" layer'. 12.3 km is well short of 40 km.

claims.claim: 'about a third of the crust' / 'ABOUT A THIRD OF THE WAY' / 'STILL IN THE CRUST'
claims.note: 12.262 / 40 = 31%, so 'about a third'. Against the 37 km peninsula average (USGS: 'average depth of the Mohorovicic discontinuity on the Kola Peninsula is 37 km with a range of 28 to 40 km') it would be 33%, still about a third.

claims.claim: 'CRUST' / '≈40 km thick here', crust drawn 40 km thick; 'MANTLE'
claims.note: 'Crustal thickness in the vicinity of the corehole was shown to be about 40 km.' The code uses CRUST_KM = 40.

claims.claim: At the bottom, the rock was over two hundred degrees.
claims.source_checked: Lobanov 2021 EN p.236 and p.238; Zhu & Huang 2026
claims.note: Lobanov: 'the real temperature in the borehole at a depth of 10 km reached 180°С, and at a depth of about 12 km, the temperature values reached 212°С, instead of the assumed 120°С'. Zhu & Huang: 'bottom-hole temperatures of 212 °C'. These are borehole measurements standing in for the rock temperature, which is the ordinary reading; the script uses 'over two hundred', not the 10 km figure. Celsius is shown on screen, not spoken.

claims.claim: '212 °C' / 'predicted: 120 °C'; thermometer 'EXPECTED: 120 °C', 'THE ROCK', '212 °C'; 'AT THE BOTTOM'
claims.note: '212°С, instead of the assumed 120°С' (p.236) and 'instead of the expected 120°С' (p.238). Both 'predicted' and 'expected' match.

claims.claim: Drilling stopped in nineteen ninety-two, when the money ran out.
claims.source_checked: Lobanov 2021 EN p.231 and p.233; Zhu & Huang 2026 (text and reference list)
claims.note: Lobanov: 'However, a drastic reduction in funding made it impossible to continue the work. Drilling was stopped in 1992.' Also p.233: 'In 1992, a unique operation was carried out to install a casing in the SG-3 borehole to continue drilling the well to a depth of 13 km. However, despite this, further drilling was abandoned.' Zhu & Huang give heat instead ('unexpectedly high bottom-hole temperatures of 212 °C induced plastic rock flow that repeatedly sealed the hole'), but their source for that paragraph is ref. 29, which is Lobanov 2021 itself, and Lobanov does not say it. So Lobanov is the better source, and 'the money ran out' is a fair plain rendering of 'a drastic reduction in funding made it impossible to continue'. Confirmed, close to the line: 'when its funding was cut' would match the source word for word.

claims.claim: '1992' then 'FUNDING CUT' (over a worn USGS bit with a red X)
claims.note: Matches Lobanov's 'drastic reduction in funding ... Drilling was stopped in 1992'. The worn bit is a USGS photo, not from Kola, and nothing on screen says it is. Framing.

claims.claim: Twelve kilometres down. The centre of the Earth is over six thousand more.
claims.note: NSSDC: 'Volumetric mean radius (km) 6371.000'. 6,371 - 12.262 = 6,359 km. Even at Kola's latitude (69°N), the radius from NSSDC's equatorial 6378.137 and polar 6356.752 km is about 6,360 km, so 'over six thousand more' holds either way.

claims.claim: '6,371 KM' / 'surface to centre'; 'THE CENTRE'; '6,000+ KM MORE'
claims.note: 6,371 km is NSSDC's volumetric mean radius. It is a mean, not the radius under Kola (about 6,360 km), but as a generic 'surface to centre' label it is the standard figure.

claims.claim: '0.2% of the way. Too thin to draw.' / 'THE HOLE: 0.2% OF THE WAY' / 'THE HOLE: TOO SMALL TO DRAW'
claims.where: on-screen: Look 1 tag; Look 2 labels; post text caption
claims.note: 12.262 / 6371 = 0.192%, which rounds to 0.2%. At the drawn radius of 310 px the hole would be 0.6 px deep, so 'too thin to draw' is accurate.

claims.claim: Earth's layers drawn from PREM: outer core radius 3,480 km
claims.where: on-screen: Look 1 planet section; SOURCES (Dziewonski & Anderson 1981)
claims.source_checked: NSSDC Earth Fact Sheet; PREM itself not reachable (data.earthscope.org/ds.iris.edu PREM_1s.csv: 403; sciencedirect: 403; EarthScope EMC-PREM.json has metadata only)
claims.note: PREM's own table could not be opened. NSSDC (A2 agency data) gives 'Core radius (km) 3485', within 0.15% of 3,480, which is 0.4 px at the drawn 310 px radius. Confirmed on NSSDC's figure, not PREM's.

claims.claim: Earth's layers drawn from PREM: inner core radius 1,221 km
claims.where: on-screen: Look 1 planet section; SOURCES (Dziewonski & Anderson 1981, 'inner core 1,221.5 km')
claims.source_checked: Tried: data.earthscope.org/app/products/portal/catalog/emc/model_pages/EMC-PREM.json (metadata only, no radii); data.earthscope.org and ds.iris.edu PREM_1s.csv (403/404); sciencedirect pii 0031920181900467 (403); api.crossref.org (title/pages only); NSSDC fact sheet (no inner core figure)
claims.note: No source meeting A2 that gives the inner-core radius could be opened. The figure is the textbook PREM value, but this pass could not confirm it. Fix by giving the checker a reachable copy of the PREM table (for example EarthScope's PREM_1s.csv) or by citing an agency page that states the inner-core radius.

claims.claim: 'CRUST', 'MANTLE', 'CORE' labels on the layers
claims.note: Framing labels for the standard layers.

claims.claim: 'DEEPEST HOLE'; 'THE KOLA BOREHOLE, USSR'; 'THE DRILL TOWER' over the 1987 Soviet stamp of the Kola well
claims.source_checked: The stamp itself (public/cutout/hole/stamp.jpg, viewed): printed 'кольская сверхглубокая скважина', 'ПОЧТА СССР', '1987', '10к'; Lobanov 2021 Fig. 2 (the enclosed derrick)
claims.note: The stamp names the Kola superdeep well and is dated 1987, USSR post. It shows a tower building and the well in section. The 'DRILL TOWER' label fits the stamp's drawing of the rig.

claims.claim: 'KOLA PENINSULA' (loop on the CIA map) and 'SOVIET UNION'
claims.source_checked: Lobanov 2021 p.227; public/cutout/hole/map.jpg with the coral loop's path mapped onto it
claims.note: Lobanov: SG-3 was laid 'in the north-western part of the Kola Peninsula, 10 km west of Zapolyarny (69°25′ N, 30°44′ E)', in the USSR. The loop drawn on the map surrounds the Kola Peninsula (Murmansk). Placement was checked against the code's coordinates, not a render.

claims.claim: 'A DRILL BIT' (museum tricone bit, 208 mm) then 'AT THE BOTTOM'
claims.source_checked: public/SOURCES.json entry for bit.jpg; Lobanov 2021 Fig. 5g
claims.note: Framing. The bit is generic ('A DRILL BIT') and not claimed to be from Kola. Kola's coring bits were carbide-tipped and of a similar size (Lobanov Fig. 5g shows one).

claims.claim: Title: 'The deepest hole ever dug never left the crust'
claims.note: Deepest (Lobanov, Zhu & Huang); stayed in a ~40 km crust (USGS).

claims.claim: Caption: 'About 20 years of drilling, 12 km down, and it got 0.2% of the way to the centre of the Earth.'
Description: 'The Kola Superdeep Borehole in the Soviet Arctic reached 12,262 metres in 1989-90, the deepest humans have ever drilled.'
claims.note: Murmansk region, 69°25′N, in the Arctic; 12,262 m; 1989 or 1990; deepest.

claims.claim: Description: 'It was drilled with a bit about 21 cm across.'
claims.note: Same as n 2: the upper 2 km was bored wider than its 325 mm casing, and the top 40 m is 720 mm. Write 'Most of it was drilled with a bit about 21 cm across' or 'Its drill bit was about 21 cm across.'

claims.claim: Description: 'The rock at the bottom was over 200 °C, against about 120 °C predicted, and the hole was about a third of the way through the crust beneath it. Funding was drastically cut, and drilling stopped in 1992.'
claims.note: 212 °C vs 120 °C assumed; 12.3 of ~40 km; 'a drastic reduction in funding made it impossible to continue the work. Drilling was stopped in 1992.'

claims.claim: SOURCES quotes of Lobanov: 'Drilling was started on May 24, 1970'; 'In 1990, the maximum depth was reached - 12262 m'; a '214 mm drill bit'; 'at a depth of 10 km reached 180°C, and at a depth of about 12 km ... 212°C, instead of the assumed 120°C'; 'a drastic reduction in funding made it impossible to continue the work. Drilling was stopped in 1992'
claims.source_checked: Lobanov 2021, the journal's English edition arcticandnorth.ru/upload/iblock/61f/44_224_239.pdf (same DOI), checked against the Russian original
claims.note: All quotes are verbatim in the English edition (lines on its pp.227, 231, 232, 236). The English edition is paginated 224-239, while SOURCES gives the Russian 267-284; the DOI is the same.

claims.claim: SOURCES quotes of Zhu & Huang: 'reaching 12,262 m between 1970 and 1989'; 'temperatures reached 180 °C at 10 km and 212 °C at 12 km'; 'Drilling was abandoned in 1992 when unexpectedly high bottom-hole temperatures of 212 °C induced plastic rock flow that repeatedly sealed the hole.'
claims.source_checked: nature.com/articles/s43247-026-03246-z (open access, Commun. Earth Environ. 7:124, online 2026-02-03)
claims.note: All three quotes are verbatim. Worth adding to SOURCES item 7: Zhu & Huang's reference for that paragraph is ref. 29, which is Lobanov 2021, and Lobanov gives funding, not heat.

claims.claim: SOURCES quotes of USGS OFR 86-517: 'Crustal thickness in the vicinity of the corehole was shown to be about 40 km'; Moho under the Kola Peninsula 37 km (range 28-40); cavities wider than 40 cm
claims.note: Verbatim: 'Crustal thickness in the vicinity of the corehole was shown to be about 40 km.' and 'The average depth of the Mohorovicic discontinuity on the Kola Peninsula is 37 km with a range of 28 to 40 km'. On cavities, the report says the neutron-gamma log shows 'a sharp drop in intensity ... where cavity diameter is greater than 40 cm', which supports the paraphrase.

claims.claim: SOURCES item 1: 'Kola Superdeep Borehole, branch SG-3'
claims.note: SG-3 is the name of the well, not a branch. The 12,262 m bore is the third shaft: 'the third one, started at a depth of 7010 m, ended at 12 262 m'. Write 'well SG-3 (the 12,262 m bore is its third branch, sidetracked at 7,010 m)'.

claims.claim: SOURCES item 2: 'The hole is not that width everywhere: below 7 km the bore went oval ... So the line and the labels name the bit'
claims.note: It leaves out that the upper hole is much wider: 720 mm to 40 m, cased at 325 mm to 2,000 m and 245 mm to 8,770 m (Lobanov Fig. 5v). And it is not true that the labels only name the bit: Look 2 labels a 21 cm disc 'THE HOLE', and Look 1 draws 'the hole seen from above' under a plate. Update after fixing n 2, n 4 and n 5.

claims.claim: SOURCES item 7: 'Lobanov describes the walls caving in instead'
claims.note: This reads as if Lobanov blames the walls caving in for the stop. He does not. He describes wall collapse in the Archean rocks as a drilling difficulty, gives the funding cut as the reason drilling stopped, and records a 1992 casing run meant 'to continue drilling the well to a depth of 13 km'. Reword, and note that Zhu & Huang's heat explanation cites Lobanov (their ref. 29), who does not say it.

claims.claim: SOURCES item 9: 9,584 m in June 1979 passing the US record of 9,583 m; 12,000 m on 27 December 1983; 12,262 m in 1989-90
claims.note: 'In June 1979, the well broke the record of 9583 meters held by the US well, reaching a depth of 9584 meters.' RU: '27 декабря 1983 г. глубина скважины достигла 12 000 м'. The animation's straight-line interpolation between these points is flagged as such in SOURCES.
